source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension (នាយកដ្ឋានផ្សព្វផ្សាយកសិកម្ម), "បច្ចេកទេសដាំដុះសណ្តែកបាយ" (Mung Bean Cultivation Techniques handbook), Kingdom of Cambodia, MAFF, published by the Department of Agricultural Extension. Reference list on the closing page cites additional 2003-dated MAFF/agricultural-extension source booklets on mung bean varieties, seed production, and pest management, plus several international references (Plant Resources of South-East Asia Vol. I, 1992; Talekar & Skinner, Field Guide to Insect Pests of Tropical Asia, 1995; Nelson, Insect Pests of Vegetables, Philippines, 1969; Mung Bean Adaptation Trial, Kbalkoh Station 1996-2000, CLV Network; and a 1991 Bangkok workshop proceedings on Yellow Mosaic Virus). No elibrary.maff.gov.kh URL is visible on the scanned pages provided, so none is given here. Uploaded as a 38-page scanned PDF; no embedded text layer, all content read visually from page images. This is Source C for crop/mung_bean in this knowledge base (Sources A-B were processed in Batch 42).
text: Mung bean can be grown across a range of soil types but performs poorly on heavy clay soil with a fine, compacted texture and low pH (the source specifies pH below 4 as problematic), which the source states causes stunted growth, reduced plant height, and low yield. The best-suited soils are loose, friable, well-drained soils with good organic-matter content, such as alluvial soils rich in humus; higher organic matter is described as improving availability of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), calcium (Ca) and magnesium (Mg). The source gives two different recommended pH ranges depending on which of the two legume types in the prior background file is being grown: the black-gram type is stated to need pH 4.8-7.5, while the mung bean/green-gram type is stated to need pH 5.5-7.0.
